question: Dani frames the comment as a joke and apologises when he names it. Why is it still gender-based harassment?

options.text: Intent doesn't determine impact — how she meant it doesn't set what it did
options.note: "It was a joke, you really can't take one" moves the problem from what she did to how he received it. That move is the harassment continuing, not ending.

options.text: She used a two-level seniority gap to make the contact and the comment
options.note: The gap is what makes the room closed even with the door open. Refusing costs him something it would never cost her.

options.text: "For a diversity hire" reframes his competence as something he was granted
options.note: It arrives attached to praise, which is what makes it hard to reject. He can't object to the compliment without objecting to the compliment.

options.text: Because she is his manager and all humour between levels is prohibited
options.note: Seniority doesn't outlaw jokes. It changes who can safely decline one, which is a narrower and more useful point.

options.text: Because he didn't laugh
options.note: Whether he laughed decides nothing. On the deflection route he laughs along, and the cost lands anyway.

options.text: Because it happened outside normal working hours
options.note: Late and empty made it easier. The same words at 11am would be the same words.

question: He asks her to take her hand off him and she does, immediately. What made the contact a boundary violation in the first place?

options.text: Consent is required before contact, not granted by the absence of objection
options.note: She never asked. Stopping when told is the minimum, not a defence — the violation was complete before he said anything.

options.text: The seniority gap made refusing expensive, so silence can't be read as permission
options.note: Naming it costs him standing in the scenario, and that isn't a game mechanic being cynical. That's the calculation he has about four seconds to do.

options.text: Stopping promptly doesn't undo it, and what follows shows why
options.note: Her embarrassment converts into something cooler within four seconds. He asked correctly, she complied correctly, and he still paid.

options.text: She held on after he asked — that's what made it a violation
options.note: She didn't. Requiring her to refuse before it counts sets the bar so high that almost nothing clears it, which is exactly why this reading is common.

options.text: It happened in a closed room rather than an open one
options.note: The closed room removed witnesses. It didn't create the problem, and an open-plan version would still be one.

options.text: Physical contact is only acceptable between people of equal seniority
options.note: Not the rule, and it implies a peer could have done this. Consent is the variable here, not the org chart.

question: Jean says "she's a lot after seven — you get used to her." What does that tell us, and what should have happened instead?

options.text: Jean already knew, which means others did too, and nobody said anything beforehand
options.note: "You get used to her" is only sayable by someone who has. This wasn't a first time; it was a first time for him.

options.text: The pattern needed naming to someone who could act on it, before he walked into that room
options.note: Bystander action isn't only about the moment. Every person who knew and treated it as a personality trait made the room he was sent into.

options.text: Framing it as something you get used to makes it his job to adapt
options.note: Said kindly, and it still hands him the work. He is now the one managing Dani's behaviour, alone, on his own time.

options.text: Warning him privately to avoid late meetings with her
options.note: Better than nothing, and it puts the whole burden on him — he now declines meetings with a principal engineer and pays for that too.

options.text: Nothing — Jean wasn't in the room, so it wasn't hers to raise
options.note: She wasn't in the room and she knew about the room. That's the definition of a bystander, not an exemption from being one.

options.text: Confronting Dani directly on his behalf
options.note: Takes the decision off him the day after somebody else already took a decision about his body.

question: He tells a colleague what happened and says he isn't sure he wants to report it. What is a trauma-informed response?

options.text: Believe him
options.note: First, and without a follow-up question that sounds like a test. Everything else is worthless without it.

options.text: Tell him it isn't his fault, particularly if he laughed along
options.note: The deflection route is the one most people take, and it's the one that leaves people most convinced they consented to it.

options.text: Let him decide what happens next, including deciding nothing happens
options.note: The scenario makes both reporting routes fail differently. Someone who's read the outcome letter can say so; nobody gets to make the choice for him.

options.text: Explain that he has a responsibility to report it so it doesn't happen to someone else
options.note: True and devastating. It makes the next person's safety his debt, on the worst day he's had, and it's the single most common thing said to people in this position.

options.text: Reassure him that Dani probably didn't mean it that way
options.note: It's an argument about her, offered to him, while he's the one who needs something.

options.text: Offer to report it for him so he doesn't have to
options.note: Generous and still a decision made over his head. Offer to go with him instead — that keeps it his.
